title: Sherlock and the Valid String
directAnswer: Build the character-frequency map, then build a frequency-of-frequencies map (how many letters share each count). A string is valid if (a) all letters already share one count, or (b) there are exactly two distinct counts and you can delete exactly one character of one letter to merge them. Case (b) holds when the smaller count is 1 occurring once (delete that lone letter), or the larger count is exactly 1 more than the smaller and occurs only once (delete one occurrence of that letter). Otherwise invalid. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.formula:
freq = Counter(s)
counts = Counter(freq.values())
if len(counts) == 1: VALID
if len(counts) == 2:
    (f1,c1),(f2,c2) = sorted(counts.items())  # f1 < f2
    VALID if (f1 == 1 and c1 == 1) or (f2 - f1 == 1 and c2 == 1)
else: INVALID
rules: Count twice: first letters → frequencies, then frequencies → how many letters have them.
One distinct frequency ⇒ already valid, no deletion needed.
Three or more distinct frequencies ⇒ **impossible** — one deletion changes only one letter's count by one.
With two frequencies, only two repair shapes work: a lone count-1 letter you can delete entirely, or a single letter whose count is exactly one above the rest.
You may delete **at most one** character total — not one per letter.
whenToUse: Asked if frequencies can be equalised by removing at most one character
Counts must all match after a single edit, and the edit is a deletion
Small fixed alphabet, so frequency-of-frequencies is tiny (O(1))
You see 'all characters appear the same number of times' as the goal
antiSignals: Allowed to delete more than one character → that's a different (k-deletion) problem
Edit is a replacement, not a deletion → Anagram-style frequency-difference instead
Need to find WHICH character to delete → track the offending letter, not just yes/no
Need the minimum deletions to make valid → count surpluses, don't just test feasibility
remember.takeaway: The trick is the second level of counting: collapse the frequency map into a frequency-of-frequencies. A valid string can have at most two distinct counts, and the gap between them must be repairable by deleting a single character — which is only true in two narrow shapes.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for a two-level count (frequency of frequencies) and then enumerate the exact handful of cases a single deletion can repair, rather than trying random deletions.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Allowing the 'delete one' to apply per-letter, or forgetting that three distinct frequencies can never be fixed; also mishandling the count-1 case (e.g. "aabbc") versus the count-too-high case (e.g. "aabbccc").
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the invariant first: 'one deletion changes exactly one letter's count by one, so a valid string has at most two distinct frequencies and the gap must be 1-with-single-occurrence — or one of the counts is a lone 1.' Then list the two repair shapes.

problemStatement:
A string is **valid** if all of its characters appear the **same number of times**. It is also valid if you can remove **exactly one character** at **one index** in the string, and the remaining characters then all appear the same number of times.

Given a string `s`, return `"YES"` if it is valid, otherwise `"NO"`.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
You may delete at most one character total (zero or one)
understanding: Two layers of counting decide everything. First, count how often each letter appears. Then count how many letters share each frequency. If every letter already has the same frequency, the string is valid as-is. Otherwise there can be at most two distinct frequencies, and a single deletion (which lowers exactly one letter's count by one, possibly to zero) must be enough to make them all equal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does 'remove exactly one character' mean I must delete, or may delete?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: May — zero deletions is allowed if the string is already valid. The 'exactly one' refers to the maximum you're permitted when a repair is needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the edit a deletion or a replacement?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A deletion: you drop one character at one index. That lowers exactly one letter's frequency by one (possibly to zero).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I delete one character from several letters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. At most one deletion total, affecting exactly one letter's count by one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the alphabet?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase a–z, so both the frequency map and the frequency-of-frequencies map are O(1) in size.

examples.explanation: Frequencies a:2, b:2, c:1, d:1 → counts {2:2, 1:2}. Two letters have count 1, so one deletion can fix only one of them; the other still breaks equality.
Frequencies a:2, b:2, c:1 → counts {2:2, 1:1}. The lone count-1 letter 'c' can be deleted entirely, leaving a:2, b:2 — all equal.
a,b,c,d,e have count 2 but f,g,h,i have count 1 → counts {2:5, 1:4}. Four lone letters means four deletions needed — more than one allowed.
Every letter appears twice except one appears three times → counts {2:?, 3:1}. Deleting one occurrence of the triple makes all counts 2.

diagrams.title: The frequency-of-frequencies decision
diagrams.caption: One distinct count is instantly valid; two may be repairable; three or more is hopeless.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Deleting Each Character
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to prove correctness intuition, then note that recomputing frequencies after each candidate deletion is wasteful.
hints: The definition is operational: 'remove exactly one character and check if the rest are uniform'. What's the most direct simulation?
First test whether the string is already valid (all frequencies equal). If not, try removing each index in turn and re-test.
Re-counting frequencies for all n candidate deletions is O(n) each → O(n²). Correct, but you can decide everything from the original counts alone.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Checking uniformity is O(n) over a 26-letter map. Trying every one of n deletions and re-checking is O(n²). The alphabet-sized maps keep space O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Simulate the definition literally. First check whether `s` is already valid: build the frequency map and confirm all non-zero counts are equal. If it is, return `"YES"`. Otherwise, for each index `i`, imagine deleting `s[i]`, rebuild the frequencies, and test uniformity; return `"YES"` the moment one deletion works.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem is phrased as an operation — 'remove exactly one character' — so the mechanical response is to perform every possible removal and check the result. It is unquestionably correct.

**Why it's wasteful.** Re-counting the entire string after each of the `n` candidate deletions repeats almost identical work `n` times. For `n = 10⁵` that's ten billion operations. Everything we learn from a deletion is already encoded in the original frequency map — deleting one copy of letter `x` just decrements `freq[x]` by one.

**The bridge to optimal.** Because a deletion only nudges one letter's count down by one, you never need to mutate the string at all. Summarising the frequency map by *how many letters share each count* tells you in O(1) whether a single decrement can equalise everything.
approaches.insight: A single deletion is fully described by 'decrement one entry of the frequency map by one'. That means you can reason about all n possible deletions from the frequency map alone, without ever rebuilding the string — which is exactly what the optimal frequency-of-frequencies approach does.

pitfalls: Rebuilding the full frequency map for every candidate deletion — O(n²).
Treating count-0 letters as breaking uniformity — ignore zeros.

approaches.name: Frequency of Frequencies (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — frame it as 'count the letters, then count those counts, then test the two repair shapes'.
hints: A deletion lowers exactly one letter's count by one. So how many DISTINCT counts can a valid string tolerate?
Build freq = count of each letter, then counts = count of each frequency value. If there's only one distinct frequency, it's already valid.

If there are exactly two distinct frequencies f1 < f2, it's valid only when f1 == 1 with a single occurrence (delete that lone letter), or f2 == f1 + 1 with a single occurrence (delete one from that letter). Any other shape, or three+ frequencies, is NO.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to build the frequency map (O(n)), then constant work over at most 26 frequency values. Both maps are bounded by the 26-letter alphabet, so space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Count letters into `freq`, then count those frequencies into `counts` (a map from 'a frequency value' to 'how many letters have it'). The number of distinct keys in `counts` decides almost everything.

**One distinct frequency → valid immediately.** Every letter already appears the same number of times; no deletion needed.

**Three or more distinct frequencies → impossible.** A single deletion changes exactly one letter's count by exactly one. That can collapse at most two frequency groups into agreement; it can never reconcile three different values. Return `"NO"`.

**Exactly two distinct frequencies f1 < f2 — only two repair shapes work:**

1. **`f1 == 1` and only one letter has it.** That lone letter appears once; delete it entirely (its count goes 1 → 0, dropping out) and every remaining letter shares frequency `f2`. Example: `"aabbc"` → counts `{2:2, 1:1}` → delete `c`.

2. **`f2 == f1 + 1` and only one letter has `f2`.** One letter sticks out by a single extra occurrence; delete one copy of it (its count goes `f2 → f1`) and all letters share `f1`. Example: `"aabbccc"` → counts `{2:2, 3:1}` → delete one `c`.

Any other two-frequency shape — two lone letters (`"aabbcd"` → `{2:2, 1:2}`), or a gap larger than one (`"aaabbbbcc"`-style) — needs more than one deletion, so it's `"NO"`.

**Why O(1) space.** Both the frequency map and the frequency-of-frequencies map have at most 26 entries regardless of `n`.
approaches.insight: The leap is the *second* level of counting. The first count tells you each letter's frequency; counting those frequencies exposes the structure a single deletion can repair. Because one deletion moves one letter by one step, a valid string is pinned to at most two frequency values with a one-step, single-occurrence gap.

java.explanation: Build the frequency-of-frequencies: how many letters share each count.
Shape 1: a single lone letter with count 1 — delete it whole.
Shape 2: one letter exactly one above the rest — delete one of its copies.

python.explanation: Second-level count: maps each frequency to the number of letters with it.
Single distinct frequency ⇒ valid with zero deletions.
Sort so f1 < f2; c1, c2 are how many letters hold each frequency.
Exactly one letter appears once — drop it; the rest already match f2.

pitfalls: Allowing the deletion per-letter — only ONE deletion total is permitted.
Forgetting that three or more distinct frequencies is always invalid.
Mixing up the two repair shapes — count-1-once (delete whole) versus gap-of-1-once (delete one copy).
Not requiring the offending frequency to occur exactly once (c1 == 1 or c2 == 1).

commonMistakes: Letting 'remove exactly one character' apply to multiple letters instead of a single deletion.
Forgetting that three or more distinct frequencies can never be repaired.
Confusing the count-1 lone-letter case with the frequency-one-too-high case.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating the deletion as per-letter
commonMistakesDetailed.why: "aabbcd" has two letters with count 1; fixing both needs two deletions. Only one deletion is allowed, so it must be NO.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# wrong: assumes any single-count letters can all be dropped
return "YES" if all(c in (1, base) for c in freq.values()) else "NO"
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if len(counts) == 2:
    (f1, c1), (f2, c2) = sorted(counts.items())
    if f1 == 1 and c1 == 1: return "YES"
    if f2 - f1 == 1 and c2 == 1: return "YES"

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the three-frequency impossibility
commonMistakesDetailed.why: One deletion shifts a single letter's count by one — it can't reconcile three different frequency values, so any counts.size() >= 3 is NO.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dropping the single-occurrence requirement
commonMistakesDetailed.why: f2 - f1 == 1 alone isn't enough; if two letters share the higher count (c2 > 1), deleting one fixes only one of them. The offending frequency must occur exactly once.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if f2 - f1 == 1 and c2 == 1:
    return "YES"

patternNote: Frequency of frequencies (two-level counting). When a problem constrains how character counts may differ — especially under a bounded number of edits — count the letters, then count those counts. The compact frequency-of-frequencies map exposes exactly which repairs a single edit can achieve.
